summary: Describes a simple method for encoding telephone numbers in the local part of email addresses, with an extension mechanism for extra attributes for gateways to telephone-based services.

plainLanguage.summary: How should a telephone number be written in the left-hand side of an email address? This document gives the minimal answer: a name for the service, an equals sign, and the number in international form, plus a fixed way for adding extra details.

questions: how to put a phone number in an email address
what is a service selector in gstn email
subtitle: A minimal way to write a telephone number inside an email address, with a registered extension mechanism.

tldr.problem: Since the first gateways between email and the telephone network appeared, implementors had invented several different ways of writing a telephone number in an email address, so a sender could not rely on any of them.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a minimal grammar for a telephone address in the local part of an email address: a service selector, an equals sign and a global phone number, with optional extension elements in a fixed slash-keyword-equals-string form. Every new service or extension has to be registered with IANA before it may be used.
tldr.outcome: Email gateways to telephone services now have one agreed format to parse, and other services can extend it without breaking that format. The document obsoletes RFC 2303 and updates RFC 2846.

facts.label: Global phone form
facts.value: A plus sign followed by digits

facts.label: Permitted separators
facts.value: Hyphen and dot, ignored by implementations

facts.label: Service selector characters
facts.value: Digits, letters and hyphen, with no space

facts.label: Registration requirement
facts.value: Specification Required, reviewed by an appointed expert

facts.label: Optional characters in the local part
facts.value: Quotes and slashes, which a gateway may strip

today: RFC 3191 is a Draft Standard from October 2001 that obsoletes RFC 2303 and updates RFC 2846, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
As with all Internet mail addresses, the left-hand side, the local part, of an address generated according to this specification is not to be interpreted except by an MTA that handles messages for the domain given in the right-hand side.

Since the very first email to GSTN services gateway appeared, implementors have used a number of different methods to specify a GSTN address as an email address. Several objectives for these methods have been identified: to enable an email user to access GSTN services from their email interface, to allow some kind of GSTN over email service transport, possibly reducing the cost of GSTN long distance transmissions, while using the existing email infrastructure.

The memo describes the minimal addressing method for encoding GSTN addresses, commonly called telephone numbers, into email addresses, together with the standard extension mechanism for encoding the additional standard attributes that email gateways to GSTN-based services need. The opposite problem, letting a traditional numeric-only GSTN device user reach the email transport service, is not discussed.

The formal definitions are given in ABNF syntax. The memo defines three new terms. An I-pstn device is a device that has an Internet domain name and is able to communicate, directly or indirectly, with the GSTN network. The mta-I-pstn is the Internet domain name that identifies an I-pstn device uniquely over the Internet. The pstn-email is the complete Internet email address structure used to transport a GSTN address over the Internet email service.

All implementations supporting the GSTN over email service must support at least the specification in this document, and the generic complex case of converting the entirety of GSTN addressing into email is out of scope in this minimal specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Every vendor had its own idea of how to write a phone number in an email address, so a message could not be routed reliably. This document settles on one minimal form and defines the terms the rest of the specification uses.

sections.title: The Minimal GSTN Address
sections.content:
The minimal specification of a GSTN address within an email address is that the address is a pstn-mbox with an optional extension element, where the pstn-mbox is a service selector, an equals sign and a global phone number. The service selector is one or more digits, letters or hyphens; a space is not allowed in it, and it must be handled as a case-insensitive string by implementations.

Other specifications that adopt the pstn-address definition must define and register with IANA a unique case-insensitive service-selector element to identify the specific messaging service involved. Those specifications and registrations must also define which minimal extension elements, if any, must be supported for the specified messaging service.

Implementations conforming to this minimal specification are allowed to ignore any other non-minimal extension element present in the pstn-address. However, conforming implementations must preserve all the extension elements they receive. The generic extension element is a slash, a keyword, an equals sign and a string, where the keyword is one or more digits, letters or hyphens with no space allowed, and the string is a printable character. All pstn-address extension elements must be defined in this form at the time of registration with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has three parts: which service, an equals sign, and the number. Anything else that a particular service needs travels in a slash-prefixed extension element, and every such element has to be registered before use.

sections.title: The global-phone Element
sections.content:
The purpose of the global-phone element is to represent standard E.164 numeric addresses within a syntax for electronic mail addressing that complies with the standard email specifications. The minimal supported syntax is a plus sign followed by one or more digits or written separators, where a written separator is a hyphen or a dot.

The use of other dialing schemes for GSTN numbers, such as private numbering plans or local dialing conventions, is also allowed. However, this does not preclude or remove the mandatory requirement for support of the global-phone syntax within the minimal GSTN address format, and any other dialing scheme must not use the leading plus sign defined here between the equals sign and the dialing string: the plus sign is strictly reserved for the standard global-phone syntax. The specification of alternate dialing schemes is out of scope for this minimal specification.

The document also permits the use of written separators in order to improve the human readability of GSTN email addresses. These separators can be placed between dial elements such as digits. Implementors' note: the use of the written separators is allowed but not recommended for transmission, and any occurrences of them in a pstn-mbox must be ignored by all conformant implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The number itself is written in international form, starting with a plus sign, then digits. Hyphens and dots may be inserted for readability, and every implementation must ignore them.

sections.title: The mta-I-pstn Part of the Address
sections.content:
An I-pstn device has, among its characteristics, a unique Internet domain name that identifies it on the Internet. Within Internet mail this is the right-hand side of the address, the part on the right of the at sign, and this document calls it the mta-I-pstn, which is simply a domain.

For domain strings used in SMTP transmissions the string must conform to the requirements of the standards for domains, and for domain strings used in message content headers it must conform to the requirements of the relevant standards. The use of domain names or domain literals is permitted in addresses in both the SMTP envelope and the message header fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The right-hand side of the address is the ordinary domain name of the machine or gateway that will handle the message, with the same rules as any other email address.

sections.title: The pstn-email Structure
sections.content:
The complete structure used to transfer a minimal GSTN address over the Internet email transport system is called the pstn-email. It is an email address conforming to the addr-spec syntax, with structure refinements that allow the GSTN number to be identified: optionally a quote character, optionally a slash, the pstn-address, optionally a slash, optionally a quote character, then the at sign and the mta-I-pstn.

Implementors' note: the optional slash characters can result from translations from other transport gateways, such as some X.400 gateways, which have included the slash as an optional element. Implementations must accept the optional slashes but should not generate them, and gateways are allowed to strip them off when converting to Internet mail addressing. The relevant standards define exactly when the optional quote characters surrounding the entire local part must be added.

In the event that a particular GSTN service requires multiple subaddresses, in any form defined by the standard specification for that GSTN service, that are associated with the same pstn-mbox, the use of multiple pstn-email elements is required. Implementors' note: the user agent may accept multiple subaddress elements for the same global-phone, but it must generate multiple pstn-mbox elements when submitting the message to the MTA.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole address is an ordinary email address whose local part carries the number. The slashes and quotes that some older gateways leave in place must be accepted but need not be produced. When a service needs more than one subaddress for the same number, each one gets its own email address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies a means by which GSTN addresses can be encoded into email addresses. Since email routing is determined by DNS data, a successful attack on DNS could disseminate tampered information, which causes email messages to be diverted via some MTA or gateway where the security of the software has been compromised.

There are several means by which an attacker might be able to deliver incorrect mail routing information to a client: compromise of a DNS server, generating a counterfeit response to a client's DNS query, and returning incorrect additional information in response to an unrelated query. Clients should ensure that mail routing is based only on authoritative answers. Once DNS security mechanisms become more widely deployed, clients should employ those mechanisms to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail goes where DNS says it goes, so an attacker who can answer DNS queries can divert a message to a machine they control. Clients should trust only authoritative answers, and use DNS security once it is widely deployed.

sections.title: IANA Registration and the Extension Mechanism
sections.content:
Because the service-selector and extension element values are extensible, they must be registered with IANA. To register either, the registration form templates in Sections 7.1 and 7.2 must be used. Any new registration must fulfil the Specification Required criteria of RFC 2434: values and their meaning must be documented in an RFC or other permanent and readily available reference, in sufficient detail so that interoperability between independent implementations is possible.

IANA must not accept registrations which are not supplemented by such a specification, or which are not fully specified according to the template forms. Where further consultation about accepting a new registration is needed, IANA should refer the matter to the Application Area Director, to be directed to the appropriate expert or IETF Working Group. After a successful registration, IANA should publish the registered element on the appropriate IANA web site and include it in the updates of the Assigned Numbers RFC series.

The template for a new service-selector asks for the name, a description of use that must include reference to Standards Track RFCs and other Standards Bodies documents and must define the use completely enough for independent implementation, any additional security considerations, and contact information. The template for a new extension element asks for the keyword name, the ABNF definition of the value, which must be self-contained and should reuse any already registered non-basic token from other extension elements, a description of use, a use restriction naming the service elements the new extension is meaningful for, or the keyword none, the security considerations, and contact information.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new may be invented in an address: every service name and every extension keyword has to be registered first, with a written specification detailed enough that two independent implementations would agree, and a named expert reviews each request.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2303
sections.content: There are no technical or major changes from the RFC 2303 specification, and the section records where updates and clarifications were introduced. Considering the case that telephony systems no longer conform to the single or few Public Operator paradigm, the old definition PSTN, Public Switched Telephone Network, was changed into the more adequate GSTN, Global Switched Telephone Network, although the ABNF variable names were not changed for consistency with the previous specification. It was made clear that GSTN addresses correspond in common language to telephone numbers and that the global-phone is a representation of E.164 numeric addresses. An explicit list of new terms with explanations was added to Section 1.1. The fact that any other specification adopting the pstn-address definition must register with IANA the new service-selector and extension elements was made explicit throughout the document, the relevant mechanism was added in Section 7 including the IANA registration form templates, and this is also consistent with RFC 2846. In Section 2.1 the use and meaning of the written separators was clarified. In Section 4 the quoting rules of the pstn-address and their practical use were made explicit both in the definition of the pstn-email and in the implementors' note. Section 4.1 was updated to clarify how to generate a pstn-email when more than one subaddress is used. The author's address was updated, and the references list was updated to include RFC 2846 and RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules did not change. The earlier version was tidied up: the old acronym for the telephone network was replaced, the terms were defined, the registration requirement was made explicit, and the quoting and separator rules were spelled out.

viz.caption: The three terms the document defines

items.title: I-pstn device
items.text: A device that has an Internet domain name and can communicate, directly or indirectly, with the telephone network.

items.title: mta-I-pstn
items.text: The Internet domain name that identifies an I-pstn device uniquely over the Internet.

items.title: pstn-email
items.text: The complete email address structure used to transport a telephone address over the Internet email service.

items.title: Why the local part is not interpreted
items.text: As with any email address, the left-hand side is read only by the MTA that handles messages for the domain on the right-hand side.

data.title: Minimal GSTN address
data.code:
pstn-address = pstn-mbox  [ qualif-type1 ]

pstn-mbox = service-selector "=" global-phone

service-selector = 1*( DIGIT / ALPHA / "-" )

qualif-type1 = "/" keyword "=" string

keyword = 1*( DIGIT / ALPHA / "-" )

string = PCHAR

viz.caption: The global-phone syntax and the examples from the RFC

data.title: global-phone
data.code:
global-phone = "+" 1*( DIGIT / written-sep )

written-sep = ( "-" / "." )

Examples of minimal pstn-address:

VOICE=+3940226338
FAX=+12027653000/T33S=6377
SMS=+33-1-88335215

viz.caption: The rules for registering a new element

items.title: Register before use
items.text: Every service-selector and every extension element value must be registered with IANA before it is used in an address.

items.title: A specification is required
items.text: The value and its meaning must be documented in an RFC or another permanent reference, in enough detail that two independent implementations would agree.

items.title: Use the templates
items.text: Registration requests use the forms in Sections 7.1 and 7.2, which ask for a description of use, any security considerations, contact information and, for an extension, the services it applies to.

items.title: An expert reviews it
items.text: IANA must not accept an unregistered or unspecified request, and refers questions to the Application Area Director for an expert or working group.

viz.caption: How mail routing can be tampered with

items.title: Compromise of a DNS server
items.text: An attacker who controls a name server can send the wrong routing information.

items.title: A counterfeit answer
items.text: An attacker can reply to the client's own DNS query with a false answer.

items.title: Incorrect additional information
items.text: An unrelated query can carry back additional records that a client then uses.

items.title: What clients should do
items.text: Base mail routing only on authoritative answers, and use DNS security mechanisms to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
